name: 5396-batchdecode-8bfp8-1gpu
hardware: 1x H100 80GB HBM3 (one GPU of an a3 node, --gres=gpu:1).
parallelism: TP=1, PP=1, DP=1, one engine, one GPU.
architecture: dense decoder (LlamaForCausalLM, 32 layers, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads, head_dim 128, hidden 4096, intermediate 14336, hidden_act silu, rope_theta 500000, max_position_embeddings 8192, vocab 128256, bf16 base). quantization_config `{quant_method: fp8, activation_scheme: static}`: the linear weights AND their input activations are 8-bit float on STATIC per-tensor scales, baked into the checkpoint as an `input_scale` and a `weight_scale` beside every linear (read off model.safetensors.index.json, not assumed). Norms, residuals, embeddings, lm_head and KV stay bf16, so KV is 2*32*8*128*2 B = 128 KiB per token and one 16-token block is 2 MiB. ~8.0B params at one byte plus bf16 embeddings and lm_head = ~10 GB of weights. Not substitutable: sibling checkpoints under similar names carry DYNAMIC activation scales, which is a different engine path and a different question. Llama-3 carries no bias on any projection, which matters because it is what keeps every fp8 linear on one single path through the engine rather than splitting the run across two.
load_profile: concurrent (closed loop), streams=256, warmup 10%, NO cooldown, bounded at 2048 requests with a 1800 s safety cap. CHOSEN, and the stream count is the single most consequential choice in this item -- read `chose_freely` (1) before moving it. 256 concurrent streams is the plainest way to hold the running batch at a fixed, known, LARGE value for the whole decode phase: 256 in flight means 256 rows entering every decode step, with no arrival-process jitter moving it around. THE NUMBER IS NOT ARBITRARY AND IS NOT SYMMETRIC. It is simultaneously (a) this engine's default `max_num_seqs` and (b) the last rung of its cuda-graph ladder, so it is the largest running batch that is both admitted whole and graph-replayed. Walking it DOWN is free and the search owns that direction outright. Walking it UP costs two things at once -- `max-num-seqs` has to be raised with it and the batch stops being graph-replayed -- so a point above 256 is not comparable to one at or below it and must be labelled. 2048 requests is 8 full rounds of 256 streams; the 1800 s cap is deliberately generous because a lower concurrency takes longer to retire the same 2048 requests. Seed static 5396 (the default is 42; pinning the item number makes the synthetic corpus reproducible per item).
workload: synthetic `synthetic_text`, single turn, no prefix bucket: prompt EXACTLY 128 tokens (min = max) and output EXACTLY 512 (min = max), greedy (`temperature: 0.0`), 2048 requests. CHOSEN. The shape is picked to make the run be mostly generation: 128 in and 512 out is four generated tokens for every prompt token, so each request pays one prefill step and then 512 decode steps, and essentially every forward pass in the run is a decode pass at the full 256 rows. That is what puts the run in a single, stable, HIGH-row-count regime for its whole length, and it is why the item is named `batchdecode` rather than after a short or solo decode. 512 rather than something longer because the marginal information from a longer generation is nil once the regime is stable. WIRE LENGTH IS NOT DECLARED LENGTH: the prompt is wrapped in a chat message and the checkpoint's chat template applied, so the engine sees roughly a dozen tokens more than 128 and reports the ENGINE's count. Expect ~140, not 128 exactly; that is not drift. Every request takes exactly 512 output tokens, enforced with ignore_eos. Prompts share no prefix and prefix caching is off, so every request pays its own prefill.
purpose: An 8-billion-parameter chat assistant generating long replies to short prompts for 256 concurrent users on one GPU.
launch:
# Launch config for issue item 5396-batchdecode-8bfp8-1gpu.
#
# ENGINE: the commit pinned in setupcard.md (`commit_id`). Every argument below is valid for that
#   engine and is passed straight to AsyncEngineArgs (`-` becomes `_`).
#
# Nothing here is tuned: there is no tunable.yaml and no tuned.yaml. The only thing the search owns
# is the load, which lives in scenario.json. Each line below is one of
#   (a) taken from the source's own model / hardware,
#   (b) an engine default written out so a future default cannot drift it,
#   (c) a declared choice where the source is silent -- argued in setupcard.md.

# --- SOURCE. Read off config.json and not assumed: LlamaForCausalLM, 32 layers, hidden 4096,
# intermediate 14336, 32 query heads, 8 KV heads -> head_dim 128, hidden_act silu,
# rope_theta 500000, bf16 base, max_position_embeddings 8192, vocab 128256.
# quantization_config: {"quant_method": "fp8", "activation_scheme": "static"} -- 8-bit float on
# the linear weights AND on their input activations, per-tensor, scales baked into the checkpoint
# (`input_scale` and `weight_scale` per linear). Norms, residuals, embeddings, lm_head and KV stay
# bf16, so KV is 2*32*8*128*2 B = 128 KiB per token. ~10 GB of weights.
# The exact repository matters: sibling checkpoints under similar names carry DYNAMIC activation
# scales, which is a different engine path and a different question.
model: neuralmagic/Meta-Llama-3-8B-Instruct-FP8

# --- SOURCE. One card.
tensor-parallel-size: 1

# --- SOURCE, IMPLIED. The checkpoint's own torch_dtype. The quantization scheme comes from its
# config.json and needs no argument.
dtype: bfloat16

# --- DEFAULT, PINNED. The checkpoint's own max_position_embeddings. The workload's worst case is
# 128 prompt + 512 output = 640 tokens, far inside it. Written out because on this engine it is
# what selects the batched-token default below.
max-model-len: 8192

# --- DEFAULT, PINNED. This engine's default is off, and it is left off. With it off each
# 128-token prompt is one prefill step rather than being smeared across decode steps, which is
# what keeps the decode steps this item is about uncontaminated by prefill work.
enable-chunked-prefill: false

# --- DEFAULT, PINNED. With chunked prefill off this engine computes max(max_model_len, 2048),
# i.e. 8192, in SchedulerConfig.__init__. Written out so a future default cannot drift it. It is
# what bounds a prefill step here: 8192 / 128 = 64 prompts admitted per prefill step, so the
# 256 streams fill in a few steps at the start and after that the run is decode.
max-num-batched-tokens: 8192

# --- DEFAULT, PINNED, AND LOAD-BEARING AT THIS OPERATING POINT -- read this one before moving
# the stream count. The engine default is 256 and the load profile declares 256 streams, so the
# two coincide exactly and the running batch is 256 on every decode step.
#
# 256 is ALSO the top of this engine's cuda-graph ladder: model_runner's
# `_BATCH_SIZES_TO_CAPTURE` is [1, 2, 4] + 8*i for i in 1..32, i.e. it stops at 256, and capture
# is further clipped to max_num_seqs. A running batch of exactly 256 is therefore the largest one
# this engine replays from a graph; 257 rows fall off the ladder and run eager, which changes the
# per-step host cost for a reason that has nothing to do with this item's question.
#
# THE SEARCH OWNS THE STREAM COUNT, BUT NOT FOR FREE UPWARD. Walking it DOWN is unconstrained and
# stays inside the graph ladder. Walking it UP past 256 requires raising max-num-seqs with it AND
# accepts that the batch is no longer graph-replayed, so a reading above 256 is not comparable to
# one at or below it. Any such point must say so.
max-num-seqs: 256

# --- DEFAULT, PINNED. The engine default, and what a bare `vllm serve` gives. ~10 GB of weights
# against 0.90 * 80 GB leaves roughly 60 GB of KV pool.
gpu-memory-utilization: 0.90

# --- DEFAULT, PINNED. 128 KiB/token * 16 = 2 MiB of KV per block across all 32 layers.
block-size: 16

# --- DEFAULT, PINNED. Off on this engine. The workload's prompts share no prefix, so there is
# nothing for it to hit.
enable-prefix-caching: false

# --- DELIBERATELY ABSENT:
#   enforce-eager        -- left off, so cuda graphs are captured. That is the default and the
#                           realistic serving configuration; forcing eager would change the
#                           operating point and inflate every per-step host cost. See the
#                           max-num-seqs note above for why that interacts with the stream count.
#   quantization         -- read from the checkpoint's own config.json. Naming it here would only
#                           give the engine a second chance to disagree with the file.
#   kv-cache-dtype       -- the checkpoint quantizes weights and input activations and never the
#                           KV. Quantizing KV here would move the operating point.
#   num-gpu-blocks-override
#                        -- KV is not binding: 256 streams x 640 tokens x 128 KiB is ~21 GB
#                           against a ~60 GB pool, about a third. There is no budget to pin, and
#                           nothing in this run is preempted or swapped.
#   swap-space, cpu-offload-gb, speculative-config, kv-transfer-config, enable-lora
#                        -- absent from the source and from this item's question.
#   more GPUs            -- 1 GPU is the source's own topology, not a scaling-down.
